newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia to get tough on trade barriers.
newsitem.headline: Australia to get tough on trade barriers.

text.p: Australia on Wednesday criticised major trading partners, including the United States and Japan, for restrictive trade barriers, warning it would fight hard to reverse its falling share of world exports.
In its first annual trade report, the year-old conservative government catalogued a range of barriers facing Australian exporters, including tariffs and other trade restrictions.

Trade Minister Tim Fischer said Australia would take a tougher stand against trade barriers to boost exports, worth more than A$76 billion (US$58 billion) in the year to June 30, 1996. "It is a very un-level playing field," Fischer told reporters before tabling the report in parliament.
"We are bringing a tougher, more hard-edged approach to trade liberalisation negotiations. We are about jobs here in Australia, first and foremost," he said.

Canberra plans to use the threat of complaints to the World Trade Organisation and tougher bilateral and multilateral negotiations to push key markets to cut tariffs, improve access and axe other barriers, the report said.
Australia's total market share of world exports fell to 1.1 percent in 1995 from 1.3 percent in 1989, the report said.

The report criticises barriers in some of Australia's biggest markets, including the United States, Japan, China, Indonesia, Thailand, Taiwan and South Korea. The European Union, long a target of Australian trade complaints, will be covered by a report due next year.

The report said the U.S. market was relatively open, but added strong concerns remained over access for agriculture and services exports. It also highlighted delays in certifying standards compliance and restrictions on ferry imports.
The United States is Australia's fourth largest export market, worth A$4.6 billion in the year to June 30, 1996.

The report criticised Japan, Australia's largest export market, worth A$16.4 billion in 1995/96, for high tariffs on agricultural items and restrictive regulatory, quarantine and technical measures. (A$1 = US$0.76)
